title: Setup & Mise en Place

learn.summary: Mise en place — everything in its place — is the first thing culinary school teaches: read the whole recipe, prep every ingredient, and stage your tools before heat touches a pan. Most home-cooking disasters are logistics failures, not skill failures: the garlic burns while you are still mincing the ginger. Five minutes of setup buys calm for the entire cook.

do: Before your next cooked meal, prep and bowl every ingredient and stage every tool before turning on any burner — notice the difference in stress

children.title: Essential Tools

learn.summary: You need less than you think: one 8-inch chef's knife, a large cutting board, a 10-12 inch skillet (stainless or cast iron), a heavy pot, a sheet pan, tongs, and an instant-read thermometer. A $15 thermometer eliminates more guesswork than any gadget on the market. Skip the unitaskers; buy quality on the knife and skillet first.

do: Buy an instant-read digital thermometer this week if you do not own one, and box up every kitchen gadget you have not touched in six months

children.title: Pantry Staples

learn.summary: A working pantry means dinner is always 30 minutes away: kosher salt, a neutral oil and a good olive oil, two vinegars (wine or rice, plus balsamic or sherry), soy sauce, canned tomatoes, canned beans, dried pasta, rice, onions, garlic, and a modest spice shelf. Whole spices keep about a year, ground ones fade in months. Restock the moment something runs low, not when it runs out.

do: Audit your pantry against the staples list this week, toss any ground spice older than two years, and cook one dinner entirely from what is on hand

children.title: Food Safety Temps

learn.summary: Bacteria multiply fastest between 40°F and 140°F — the danger zone — so leftovers go in the fridge within 2 hours (1 hour if it is above 90°F out). Key internal temps: poultry and reheated leftovers 165°F, ground meats 160°F, whole cuts of beef and pork 145°F plus a 3-minute rest, fish 145°F. Fridge at or below 40°F; never thaw meat on the counter.

do: Check your fridge with a thermometer this week (target 37-40°F) and tape the key internal temps inside a cabinet door

children.title: Clean As You Go

learn.summary: Professional kitchens stay clean during service, not after it: wipe the board between tasks, drop used tools into a soapy sink, and use downtime — while water boils, while onions sweat — to reset your station. A separate board (or a wash between) for raw meat versus produce prevents cross-contamination. Ending a cook with a clean kitchen is a skill, and it is learnable in a week.

do: During your next cook, fill the sink with hot soapy water before you start and wash tools during every pocket of waiting time — aim to finish dinner with an empty counter
